one_liner: Open-source lock-free Bw-Tree (concurrent B+-tree multimap) from CMU; its own benchmarks show it slower than std::map and stx::btree.
what_it_does: An independent C++11 reimplementation of Microsoft Research's Bw-Tree (the 'OpenBw-Tree'), built at CMU for the Peloton DBMS: a lock-free in-memory ordered index that lets many threads insert, delete and look up concurrently without latches. The API is a templated multimap, BwTree<Key, Value, KeyComparator, KeyEqualityChecker, KeyHashFunc, ValueEqualityChecker, ValueHashFunc>, with Insert(k, v) and Delete(k, v) returning bool, GetValue(k, std::vector<V>&) and a forward iterator from Begin() or Begin(key). There is no operator[], find, size() or in-place update, so it is not a std::map or BerkeleyDB drop-in, and operations are atomic but not isolated: transactions need a separate concurrency-control layer.
how_it_is_fast: Nodes are addressed through a mapping table of logical node IDs. Writers prepend delta records (insert, delete, split, merge) to a node's delta chain and publish them with one compare-and-swap on that node's slot, and threads 'help along' unfinished structure modifications instead of waiting on latches. A chain is consolidated into a new base node after 8 deltas, and nodes split above 128 entries and merge below 32. On top of Microsoft's design, the SIGMOD'18 paper adds delta records pre-allocated inside the base node's memory chunk, decentralized per-thread epoch GC, fast consolidation, node-search shortcuts using delta offsets, and non-unique key support; together these give 1.1-2.5x over a good-faith original Bw-Tree, but the indirection and delta-chain traversal still cost more instructions and cache misses than a latch-based B+Tree.
when_to_use: Research or teaching where you need a working lock-free Bw-Tree (mapping table, delta chains, help-along SMOs, epoch GC) to study, instrument or port to another language.

As a baseline in an index benchmark, or to reproduce or extend the SIGMOD'18 'Building a Bw-Tree Takes More Than Just Buzz Words' results (YCSB-style Insert-only, Read-only, Read/Update and Scan/Insert on integer or email keys).

A prototype that specifically requires a latch-free, comparator-based, non-unique (multimap) ordered index over small trivially-copyable keys such as 64-bit integers, where you run a fixed thread pool registered up front and stay well under the ~1M-node mapping-table cap.
when_not_to_use: Whenever speed is the reason. The repo's own single-threaded benchmark-all screenshot shows 4.65M inserts/s and 9.58M reads/s, against 5.91M/17.85M for std::map and 10.60M/21.50M for stx::btree. With 20 threads in SIGMOD'18, ART with optimistic lock coupling was more than 4x faster on point lookups, and a B+Tree with optimistic lock coupling and Masstree were often about 2x faster (3.7x for B+Tree on monotonic insert-only).
High-contention appends such as monotonic keys from many threads: in SIGMOD'18 it saw more than 10 CAS aborts per insert, and lock-based Masstree, ART and B+Tree held up better.

Large or growing indexes: the mapping table is a fixed std::array of 2^20 node IDs with no resizing (a README 'Known Problem'; issue #45 still open). That caps the tree at roughly tens of millions of keys at 32-128 entries per leaf. The SIGMOD'18 paper describes lazily-backed virtual-memory expansion, but that is not what master ships.

std::string or other non-POD keys and values: issue #62 (a segfault during the first GC cycle with std::string keys) was never fixed, and the author notes that the tree moves keys and values often, so non-POD types are slow.

Production systems. Delete is not wait-free: a thread that dies between posting and removing its ABORT delta blocks all writes under that parent (#40). There is an unfixed use-after-free race in epoch cleanup (#69), and a question about Microsoft's Bw-Tree patents (#71) was never answered. It is in-memory only, with no persistence (#72), unlike the BerkeleyDB baseline.

integration.dependencies: none for the index itself (C++11 STL plus pthreads; bwtree.h also includes sorted_small_set.h, bloom_filter.h and atomic_stack.h). The test/benchmark harness uses PAPI (disable with -DNO_USE_PAPI) and jemalloc via LD_PRELOAD, and the full-speed make target links boost_system and boost_thread.
integration.min_toolchain: C++11. Only g++-5 is used in the Makefile and Travis. clang++ fails on private nested-class access unless patched (#64). The 'register' keyword in bloom_filter.h is invalid in C++17 (#70). Needs -mcx16 for the 16-byte CAS.
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux is the only tested platform (Travis on Ubuntu). It relies on a 16-byte std::atomic CAS (LOCK CMPXCHG16B) and GCC builtins and attributes. Other architectures, macOS/Windows and MSVC are not documented.
integration.thread_safety: Insert, Delete, GetValue and iterator creation are lock-free and safe from many threads. Each thread needs a GC slot, either via RegisterThread() before the tree is constructed or via UpdateThreadLocal(n) plus AssignGCID(id). A single iterator object must not be shared between threads. Operations are atomic, not isolated.

gotchas: Debug mode is the default. Unless you compile with -DBWTREE_NODEBUG, BWTREE_DEBUG enables assertions and per-operation atomic counters, and bwt_printf logs every call to stderr while print_flag is true, which is its initial value in bwtree.cpp. ALL_PUBLIC is also hard-defined, so internal members are public.

A BwTree object is about 16 MB, because the mapping table and the free NodeID stack are in-object arrays. Declaring one on the stack crashes (#65), so always allocate it with new. The constructor also starts a background epoch/GC thread unless you pass start_gc_thread = false.

Not header-only: you must compile src/bwtree.cpp (it defines print_flag, the thread_local gc_id and the thread counter). A thread with no assigned GC ID (gc_id = -1) trips an assert or causes undefined behavior. The GC slot count is captured when the tree is constructed.

Multimap semantics: Insert only fails if that exact (key, value) pair already exists, so repeated keys accumulate values, and there is no update, so 'replace' means a non-atomic Delete + Insert. Iterators copy one leaf page at a time and give no snapshot across pages.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: For real concurrent in-memory indexing, pick ART Synchronized: the SIGMOD'18 authors measured ART with optimistic lock coupling more than 4x faster than this tree on point lookups, and LIPP's evaluation also lists BwTree among the indexes it beats. Choose Open BwTree only when the requirement is specifically a latch-free, comparator-based B+-tree multimap, or a reference implementation of the Bw-Tree/Hekaton design.
verified_claims_summary: The BerkeleyDB wins are not this code: ICDE'13's 10.40M vs 0.56M ops/s (about 18.7x, Xbox LIVE trace), 3.83M vs 0.66M (5.8x, synthetic) and 8.6x (deduplication) were measured on Microsoft's unreleased implementation on a Xeon W3550 with 8 threads. This repo's own numbers put it behind the incumbents: a single-threaded benchmark-all screenshot (g++ -O3, jemalloc, sequential long keys, a ThinkPad T440s per the shell prompt, libstdc++ inferred) shows it slower than std::map, std::unordered_map and stx::btree, and the authors' SIGMOD'18 evaluation (2x Xeon E5-2680 v2, g++ 5.4, tcmalloc) finds it 1.1-2.5x faster than a reimplemented original Bw-Tree but slower than B+Tree-OLC, Masstree and ART, ahead only of a lock-free SkipList.
status_note: Abandoned since 2018-11-14, with 14 open issues (use-after-free race, std::string segfault, clang build failure) unanswered; it is Apache-2.0 and small enough to vendor (CMU's now-archived NoisePage vendored it under third_party/bwtree), and the last known-good toolchain is g++-5 on Ubuntu.
